extracted.intended_audience: software engineering / HCI / CSCW researchers and practitioners interested in code review, feedback, and diversity/inclusion
extracted.subtask_short: empirical study of code review criticism
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical, vignette-based survey study that measures perceptions, frequency, and perceived impact of destructive versus constructive criticism in software code review, with analysis of gender and other demographic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined (citing Baron [10]) as negative feedback that is both nonspecific and inconsiderate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the paper this construct is the primary lens for analysis. Destructive criticism is hypothesized to provoke negative reactions (reduced mood, motivation, productivity) and to possibly impact women more strongly for some tasks. Use this combined definition (nonspecific + inconsiderate) when identifying destructive criticism; examples used in vignettes include comments like “This is seriously obtuse.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonspecific negative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative feedback that lacks specific improvement suggestions or actionable detail (example: “This is a hack”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized in survey questions asking past-year frequency of receiving/giving nonspecific negative feedback across academic, open source, and commercial projects. Distinguish nonspecific feedback from feedback that contains concrete suggestions for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsiderate negative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative feedback delivered in a harsh or sarcastic tone, including threats or attributions of poor performance to personal flaws (example: “You have to be stupid to do this”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one half of the destructive criticism definition. Surveyed for frequency separately from nonspecific feedback. In vignettes, inconsiderate wording is used to evaluate perceived appropriateness and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative feedback that is considerate and provides specific improvement suggestions (example in vignette: “You don’t need to protect instanceOf against null pointers”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the comparator to destructive criticism in vignette experiments; treat constructive feedback as negative-but-actionable and considerate when categorizing comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived helpfulness / improves code quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item: agreement with the statement “This feedback would help me to improve the code.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on a 5-point Likert (Strongly disagree to Strongly agree, plus I don’t know). Used to assess perceived utility of a comment (part of RQ1/RQ3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item: agreement with the statement “This feedback is valid.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on a 5-point Likert; used to capture whether participants consider the content of feedback to be factually or technically correct, independent of tone or specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item: agreement with the statement “This feedback is appropriate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on a 5-point Likert; used to assess social acceptability/fit of the feedback in code review context and to compare responses across genders and demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mood measurement (MDMQ subset)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rate mood states (good; bad; nervous; tense; great; composed; uncomfortable; at ease) after reading the vignette, using a provided response format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subset of the Multidimensional Mood Questionnaire used to capture emotional reaction to feedback. Employed to measure immediate affective impact of constructive vs destructive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to continue working
rubrics_metrics.description: Three survey items asking how motivated participants would be to: continue working on this task; continue working with this developer; continue working on this project (response scale: Very unmotivated to Very motivated, plus I don’t know).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as behavioral-intent proxies for impact (RQ3). Responses analyzed across demographic predictors to detect differential impact (e.g., by gender).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of giving/receiving code review feedback (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item: In the past year, how often have you received/given code review comments? Response options: Never; Once or more a year; Once or more a quarter; Once or more a month; Once or more a week; N/A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as baseline activity measures and as independent variables in models predicting frequency of destructive criticism; collected separately for academic, open source, and commercial projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of receiving/giving nonspecific negative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item specifically asking how often participants have received/given nonspecific negative feedback in the past year, with the same frequency response options and project-type breakdown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to quantify prevalence of nonspecific aspects of destructive criticism (RQ2). Analyzed by project type and demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of receiving/giving inconsiderate negative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item specifically asking how often participants have received/given inconsiderate negative feedback in the past year, same response options and project-type breakdown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to quantify prevalence of the inconsiderate aspect of destructive criticism (RQ2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion items on destructive criticism (harmfulness & acceptability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey items such as “Destructive criticism is harmful” and “Destructive criticism will cause a negative reaction for the recipient,” plus items about when writing and receiving comments (e.g., tradeoff: improve code quality vs avoid causing negative reaction; willingness to accept inconsiderate feedback if it improves code quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5-point Likert response options; used to capture normative beliefs and trade-offs practitioners make about code quality vs interpersonal effects (RQ1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vignette design and randomization
rubrics_metrics.description: Two vignettes per participant, each with the same code snippet and scenario description, randomized so each participant saw one constructive and one destructive feedback vignette (order counterbalanced so roughly half see destructive first). Code snippets and feedback drawn from real open-source comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vignettes standardize scenarios while preserving ecological validity; randomization ensures within-subject comparison and counterbalances order effects. Integrate code snippet into the vignette for clarity (a change made after piloting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation (priming) question
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial question presenting a code snippet with an obvious novice-level mistake asking participants to write a code review comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prepare participants to think in the code review mindset prior to vignettes; ensures engagement and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire structure and optionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Five-section questionnaire: preparation question, vignette-style questions, experience questions, opinion questions, and demographics (including self-efficacy). All questions were optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for completion in under 15 minutes; optionality reduces coercion but may lead to missing data—report counts per question and handle in analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question wording and response scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete example items and clearly defined response options (e.g., Likert scales, enumerated frequency categories, free-text optional responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clarity by piloting; include an I don’t know option where appropriate; present examples (e.g., examples of nonspecific vs inconsiderate feedback) to aid consistent interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot testing and instrument refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Piloted survey with domain-experienced participants (3 fourth-year software engineering students), used feedback to reorder questions and integrate code snippets into vignettes to improve flow and clarity; pilot respondents not included in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot with representative participants, iterate on flow and presentation, and confirm completion time target (<15 minutes). Document changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-world data for vignettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Code snippets and feedback examples used in vignettes were obtained from actual code review comments and real open-source code to ensure realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing vignettes from real interactions increases ecological validity and face validity of scenarios; document sources and examples used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographics and control measures (including self-efficacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect gender (open-ended), years of experience, highest education, self-reported competence, current occupation, age, number of OSS contributions, and a standardized self-efficacy assessment (average across eight questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as covariates in regression models to control for confounding; note potential multicollinearity (age highly correlated with years of experience in this study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment / sampling approach and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Convenience sampling via social media (Twitter, LinkedIn) and local communities/meetups; no enforced cut-off criteria but participants reported having some development experience; survey open for two months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convenience sampling is practical but introduces selection bias; document recruitment channels and participant inclusion criteria; acknowledge generalizability limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous online questionnaire with ethics approval from the University Human Participants Ethics Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain institutional ethics approval, ensure anonymity and voluntary participation, and make all questions optional to reduce harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling and analytic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary models used ordinal logistic regression for ordered Likert outcomes; a log-log model was used for a non-normally distributed frequency variable. Independent variables included gender, highest education, years experience, self-efficacy score, self-reported competence, OSS contribution, student status, and frequency-of-feedback covariates where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select regression appropriate to outcome distribution (ordinal vs continuous/non-normal). Test for multicollinearity (VIF), report VIFs, and assess goodness-of-fit (Pulkstenis-Robinson chi-squared for ordinal models). Report and bold significant predictors; investigate model fit issues and potential omitted variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness-of-fit and multicollinearity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Pulkstenis-Robinson chi-squared test to assess fit of ordinal regression models and compute variance inflation factors (VIF) to check multicollinearity among independent variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report p-values from fit tests and VIFs; if model lacks fit, acknowledge possible missing predictors or nonlinearities (the paper notes four models with evidence of lack of fit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative open-ended response capture and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants asked what they would write in response to the vignette feedback (optional free-text). Open-ended responses were used to illustrate conflicting views (e.g., some said harsh feedback is necessary; others said inconsiderate feedback is never acceptable). The paper references thematic analysis methods (Braun & Clarke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include free-text prompts to capture reasoning and nuance; analyze with established qualitative methods (e.g., thematic analysis), and report illustrative quotes and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and reporting transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly report sample sizes (e.g., n=93; gender breakdown: 43 women, 43 men, 3 non-binary), small subgroup sizes (non-binary n=3), optional-question missingness, and models with lack of fit. Discuss implications for generalizability and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about sample composition and statistical limitations (small cell sizes, optional responses); avoid overgeneralizing subgroup results when n is very small; include discussion of threats to validity.
